constitutive_assumptions: Individual layers behave elastically and orthotropically with respect to layer boundaries, sharing a constant elastic modulus E.
Bernoulli hypothesis holds for each individual layer: plane sections remain plane, resulting in linearly varying normal stresses across the layer thickness.
Shear deformations within individual layers are neglected.
Shear stress varies parabolically through the thickness of each individual layer/beamlet according to standard engineering beam theory.
Interfaces are frictionally coupled: displacements are continuous across an interface as long as shear stress is below interfacial shear strength tau_p.
Once interfacial shear stress reaches tau_p, tangential displacement discontinuity (relative slip) occurs, and interfacial shear stress remains constant at tau_p during sliding.
Normal displacements remain strictly continuous across interfaces with no interfacial opening or layer separation.
Identical layer thicknesses h and uniform, constant interfacial shear strength tau_p across all interfaces.
control_variables: Rectangular beam cross-section with width b, total height H, and n discrete layers of thickness h = H/n.
Simply-supported three-point bending configuration with a monotonically increasing central transverse point load P.
Symmetry about the midspan (x = 0) and the neutral axis (y = 0).
Beam aspect ratio L/H = 5, layer count n = 16, and overhang ratio D/L = 0.267 for primary numerical evaluations.
Dimensionless material parameter ratio tau_p / E = 30 MPa / 130 GPa = 2.308 x 10^-4 used for deflection calculations.
dependent_variables: Slip initiation loads P_si and complete-slip loads P_Ci for each interface i.
Locations and spatial extents of interfacial slip zones (boundaries A_K, B_K, and slip zone half-lengths R_i or r_i = R_i / L).
Number of beamlets m and beamlet boundaries across defined longitudinal sections.
Layer and beamlet stress resultants (axial forces N_i, N_j; bending moments M_i, M_j; shear forces V_i, V_j).
Axial normal (bending) stress distributions sigma(x, y) and peak layer axial stresses S_i,max.
Interfacial and layer shear stress distributions tau(x, y).
Beam vertical deflection profile w(x) and normalized mid-point deflection w(0)/H.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Weak longitudinal shear strength in layered materials leads to severe bending stress enhancement when transverse loading causes interfacial frictional slipping.

Under three-point bending, interfacial slip initiates at the central interface and propagates towards outer interfaces at load levels significantly lower than predicted by solid-beam shear stress profiles due to stress redistribution.

Interfacial slip allows individual layers to deform independently, producing local compressive stresses on the tensile side of the beam and magnifying maximum tensile and compressive axial stresses by multiple times compared to a solid beam.

An unconstrained beam overhang extending beyond the supports carries internal layer axial forces and moments, which stiffens the beam and significantly mitigates central deflection and peak bending stresses.

future_work: Presenting Part II containing a simplified continuum theory for a shear-weak unlayered beam to circumvent the computationally demanding discrete-layer analysis (pages 1, 2, 12).
Demonstrating the formal equivalence between the discrete slipping-layers model and the shear-weak unlayered continuum beam model as the number of layers n becomes large (pages 1, 2).
Investigating the detailed dependence of bending stress enhancement on layer count n and span-to-depth aspect ratio L/H in Part II (page 8).
Using the simplified theory in Part II to infer practical levels of bending stress enhancement expected in physical composite materials (pages 1, 12).
independent_variables: Dimensionless applied load p = P / P_s8 (or load P).
Overhang ratio d = D/L (ratio of extension beyond supports D to span L).
Number of discrete layers n (evaluated at n = 16).
Span-to-depth aspect ratio L/H (evaluated at L/H = 5).
Ratio of interfacial shear strength to Young's modulus tau_p / E.
Longitudinal coordinate x (or normalized coordinate xi = x/L) and transverse coordinate y.
limitations_inferred: The model is formulated exclusively for monotonic loading, meaning frictional hysteresis, cyclic loading, slip reversal, and wear at the interfaces are not addressed.
The frictional slip criterion assumes a constant shear threshold tau_p that is decoupled from local transverse normal compressive stress, which differs from pressure-dependent Coulomb friction.
Transverse shear deformation across the beam depth and through-thickness normal stresses are neglected, which may introduce inaccuracies in short, deep beams (e.g., L/H = 5).
No experimental testing is performed within the study to quantitatively validate the numerically predicted stress enhancement factors against physical specimens.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The discrete slipping-layers beam model is extremely computationally intensive and time-consuming to solve, even for simple loading conditions (pages 1, 2, 12).
The authors were unable to find a general solution method for general distributed transverse loads q(x) due to the difficulty of tracing the locus of multiple slip zones per interface (page 8).
Each layer is treated using the simplest beam theory (Bernoulli hypothesis) and shear deformations within layers are neglected (pages 3, 12).
Normal separation or delamination opening between layers is not permitted (pages 3, 12).
The detailed numerical calculations are limited to three-point bending with identical layer thicknesses, identical moduli, and uniform interfacial properties (pages 3, 8).

The very high stress enhancements that arise when slip extends to the specimen edges may correspond to loading regimes where the composite would in practice already be considered to have failed in shear (page 12).
main_results: Bending stresses in beams with low longitudinal shear resistance become substantially magnified once interfacial shear slippage occurs, reaching nearly four times the maximum stress of an equivalent solid beam in Stage II and continuing to escalate in Stages III and IV.

Interlayer slip alters the through-thickness normal stress profile such that individual layers experience distinct local bending, resulting in local compressive stresses appearing even on the tensile side of the beam.

In three-point bending of a 16-layer beam, slip initiates first on the central interface at load P_s8 = 4*b*H*tau_p/3; subsequent slip on outer interfaces initiates at loads substantially lower than expected from unlayered beam theory (e.g., P_s1/P_s8 = 1.531 vs. 4.267) because inner slip transfers higher shear stresses outward.

Portions of the beam extending past the supports (overhang D) carry non-zero layer bending moments and axial forces despite zero net cross-sectional resultants, leading to curvature in the overhang rather than rigid-body displacement.

Increasing the overhang ratio D/L stiffens the structure and decreases both mid-point deflection and maximum axial stress, because frictional slip generates opposing axial forces that resist the applied bending moment.
modeling_methods: Discrete slipping-layers beam theory treating the cross-section as n elastic layers coupled by frictional interfaces with finite shear strength tau_p.
Application of the generalized Bernoulli hypothesis ('plane sections remain plane') to each layer individually, yielding linear normal stress and parabolic shear stress profiles.
Section and beamlet partitioning technique demarcated by slip zone endpoints and external concentrated load locations.
Formulation of equilibrium equations for individual beamlets and continuity of vertical deflection and curvature derivatives across non-slipping and slipping interfaces.
Enforcement of continuity of layer axial forces, bending moments, and normal stresses across section boundaries.
Integral continuity condition requiring zero net tangential relative displacement across each slip zone.
Exploitation of beam symmetries (about x = 0 and y = 0) and numerical resolution of non-linear slip zone extents using Powell's optimization method under monotonically incremented loading.
performance_metrics: Normalized maximum axial stress ratio S_i,max / sigma_max (layer peak axial stress divided by the maximum axial stress in a solid beam under identical load).
Dimensionless slip initiation load ratios P_si / P_s8 and complete slip load ratios P_Ci / P_s8.
Normalized midspan deflection w(0) / H.
Normalized half-length of interfacial slip zones r_i = R_i / L.
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrating that interlayer friction and overhang geometry govern bending stiffness and stress distribution provides a theoretical basis for designing friction-based variable stiffness systems (such as layer jamming), although practical robotic implementations would require extending the model to controllable normal pressures and cyclic loading.

Because discrete slipping-layer formulations are computationally expensive, there is a clear methodological gap for homogenized continuum models capable of rapidly predicting stiffness and stress changes in real-time continuum robot mechanics.

paper.research_problem: Enhanced bending stresses and reduced load-bearing capacity occurring in materials with low longitudinal shear strength (such as weakly bonded continuous fiber ceramic-matrix composites) due to shear slippage along weakly coupled internal layers during bending.
paper.title: BENDING STRESS ENHANCEMENT IN MATERIALS WITH LIMITED SHEAR RESISTANCE-PART I. SLIPPING-LAYERS MODEL

constitutive_assumptions: Maximum sustainable shear stress on axes parallel and normal to the beam axis is capped at tau_p (shear strength), corresponding to classical perfect plasticity with infinite anisotropy.
Normal stresses along axes parallel and normal to the beam axis are assumed to be unlimited.

Net axial force across the cross-section is zero.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: An unlayered shear-weak beam model based on perfect plasticity with infinite anisotropy provides a simplified continuum representation of bending stress enhancement without the high computational burden of discrete layered beam models.
When transverse shear force exceeds V_p = 2 b H tau_p / 3, a plastic zone of thickness Hp = (3 V/V_max - 2) H develops where shear stress equals tau_p and normal stress is zero.
Once the plastic shear threshold is exceeded, the surface tensile stress exceeds elastic beam theory predictions and grows unbounded as shear force approaches V_max = b H tau_p.
Beam curvature in the shear-weak beam is enhanced by the same shear-dependent factor as surface stress, altering bending compliance under simultaneous shear and moment.
As the number of discrete slipping layers n approaches infinity, the discrete slipping-layer equations asymptotically converge to the unlayered shear-weak beam model.

Discrepancies in predicted shear force and surface tensile stress between discrete-layer and unlayered models diminish as the number of layers increases and are smaller for smaller plastic zone sizes.
Under identical loads, the unlayered shear-weak model yields an upper-bound estimate of surface stress enhancement compared to beams with a finite number of slipping layers.
Simultaneous high bending moment and high shear force establish a reduced failure locus in (V/V_max, M/M_max) space, causing surface tensile failure at moments lower than M_max.
In three-point bending, apparent flexural strength is reduced for beams with length-to-height aspect ratios L/H below (L/H)* = sigma_max / (2 tau_p), rendering short beams apparently weaker.

The impact of shear weakness is highly sensitive to loading configuration, being severe under three-point bending where peak moment coincides with peak shear, and minimal under distributed loads where peak moment occurs at zero shear.

experimental_setup: No new experimental testing was conducted in this study; the investigation is purely theoretical and analytical.

Theoretical results are compared with trends from existing external experimental data by Prewo and Nardone (1986) on three-point bending of carbon-fiber reinforced glass matrix composites across varying aspect ratios.
future_work: Detailed quantitative comparison between the unlayered shear-weak model predictions and experimental results on carbon-fiber reinforced glass matrix composites is indicated as reported in a companion work (Steif and Trojnacki, 1992).
Simultaneous determination of stress resultants and deflections in statically indeterminate beam configurations.
independent_variables: Normalized transverse shear force V/V_max (or V/V_p)
Dimensionless applied load p = 3P / (4 b H tau_p) in three-point bending
Number of discrete layers n in layered beam comparisons
Beam length-to-height aspect ratio L/H
Material strength ratio sigma_max / tau_p
Loading type and distribution (three-point concentrated bending vs. uniformly distributed transverse loading)
limitations_inferred: The constitutive formulation assumes rigid-perfect or elastic-perfect shear yield behavior without work hardening, rate sensitivity, or viscoelastic/viscoplastic response.
The beam theory is two-dimensional and does not account for cross-sectional warping, transverse normal stresses through the thickness, or out-of-plane stress components.
Local stress concentrations, contact indentation beneath concentrated point loads, and specific micro-mechanical failure modes (e.g., matrix cracking, fiber microbuckling) are not modeled.
The analysis is strictly developed for structural mechanics of composite beams and does not incorporate robotic actuation, flexible kinematic linkages, or large-displacement kinematics.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Modeling fiber composites as discrete layers is computationally intensive and at best an approximation.

The shear-weak beam model can sustain loads only up to V_max = b H tau_p, meaning comparisons with discretely layered beams become poor when shear force approaches or exceeds V_max (since layered beams have no theoretical load ceiling).
Setting sigma = 0 and tau = tau_p in the plastic zone is an idealized constitutive assumption justified primarily by its quantitative agreement with discrete slipping-layer results.
The normal component of stress transverse to the beam axis is neglected in accordance with elementary beam theory approximations.
The impact of shear weakness depends strongly on the loading conditions and is minimal when maximum bending moment and maximum shear force do not coincide.
main_results: Formulated a closed-form continuum model for shear-weak beams where the plastic core thickness is explicitly defined by Hp = (3 V/V_max - 2) H for shear forces exceeding V_p = 2 V_max / 3.
Demonstrated that surface tensile stress S_max is enhanced by factor [1 - 2/3 (V/V_max)] / [1 - V/V_max] for V > V_p, diverging as V approaches V_max.
Proved that the discrete slipping-layer model from Part I asymptotically converges to the unlayered shear-weak model as the number of layers n approaches infinity.
Showed that quantitative discrepancies between the layered and unlayered models decrease monotonically as n increases and are smaller for smaller plastic zone thicknesses.
Established a combined failure envelope in (V/V_max, M/M_max) space showing that concurrent shear force reduces the sustainable bending moment before reaching tensile strength.

Demonstrated that apparent flexural strength in three-point bending decreases for aspect ratios below (L/H)* = sigma_max / (2 tau_p), consistent with experimental observations in fiber-reinforced brittle composites.
Showed that shear weakness effects are minimal in load cases where maximum moment occurs at zero shear (e.g., simply supported beams under uniform transverse loading).
modeling_methods: Unlayered shear-weak beam continuum model based on classical perfect plasticity with infinite anisotropy (Hill, 1948).
Piecewise cross-sectional stress formulation dividing the section into an inner plastic core (tau = tau_p, sigma = 0) and outer elastic regions governed by modified beam theory.
Equilibrium and cross-sectional strain continuity conditions used to determine the plastic boundary Hp(x) and surface stress enhancement.
Curvature calculation through integration of axial strain variation across the elastic beam portion.
Asymptotic limit analysis (n -> infinity) of a third-order algebraic equation governing slipping interfaces in discretely layered beams.
Bending moment versus shear force failure locus modeling for combined loading states.
performance_metrics: Percentage error e1 = [V - V*(n*)] / V*(n*) for shear force required to achieve a given plastic zone size.
Percentage error e2 = [S_max - S_max^n] / S_max^n for maximum surface tensile stress between unlayered and layered models.
Stress enhancement ratio S_max / sigma_max^e (ratio of maximum tensile stress to elastic beam theory stress).
Normalized failure load ratio P / P_max in three-point bending.
Critical length-to-height aspect ratio threshold (L/H)* = sigma_max / (2 tau_p).
possible_gap_implications: The unlayered shear-weak continuum approach provides a potential mechanics framework to model shear compliance and bending-shear interaction in layered or fiber-reinforced flexible structural elements, but requires extension to finite deformation kinematics before it can be applied to large-deflection continuum robots or soft grippers.

The failure surface under coupled shear and bending highlights that flexible continuum structures subjected to concentrated transverse forces must account for shear-induced bending stress enhancement to prevent premature tensile failure.
paper.research_objective: To present a simple continuum model for an unlayered beam weak in shear, quantitatively compare its predictions with the discrete slipping-layer beam model of Part I, and evaluate the effects of limited shear resistance on bending stress enhancement, failure envelopes under combined loading, and beam aspect ratio in bending.
paper.research_problem: Fiber composites can experience severe bending stress enhancement due to limited shear resistance, but analyzing such materials using discrete slipping-layer models is computationally intensive and represents an approximation of actual composite behavior.
paper.title: Bending Stress Enhancement in Materials with Limited Shear Resistance-Part II. Unlayered Shear-Weak Model

constitutive_assumptions: The layer material is assumed to be isotropic and linear elastic.

Couple and moment stresses are assumed to be proportional to the relative deformation gradient rather than microstructural rotation gradients alone, so moment stresses vanish in pure bending when interfacial slip is absent.
The moment-curvature constitutive relation is assumed ad hoc such that m = -[E h^3 / (12(1 - nu^2))] * kappa^rel, where kappa^rel = -u_{1,21} + omega_{3,1}^c.

Interfaces exhibit two behavioral modes: elastically connected with normal and shear interface stiffnesses (k_n and k_s), and disconnected with frictional sliding modeled using an elasto-plastic yield criterion f = |sigma_{12}| + sigma_{22} tan(phi) - c <= 0 and plastic potential g = |sigma_{12}|.

In the incremental virtual work formulation for large deformations, geometric nonlinearities associated with higher-order deformation gradient derivatives and higher-order stresses are assumed negligible.

For the layered beam example, rotations are assumed large compared to strains in accordance with technical beam and plate buckling theories, using standard kinematic assumptions u_1 = -x_2 Omega(x_1), u_2 = v(x_1), and omega_3^c = Omega^c(x_1).

The thickness parameter h in the continuum formulation is treated as an effective scale-dependent renormalized parameter defined via observed macroscopic moduli rather than strictly the physical lamination thickness.
control_variables: Beam center deflection study: Poisson's ratio nu = 0, aspect ratio t/L = 0.2, thickness ratio h/t = 0.2, initial axial stress sigma_0 = 0, distributed transverse load q = 0.
Compliance test study: Poisson's ratio nu = 0, aspect ratio t/L = 0.2, thickness ratio h/t = 0.2.
Buckling study: Poisson's ratio nu = 0.2, aspect ratio t/L = 0.25, thickness ratio h/t = 0.1, transverse load P = 0, distributed load q = 0.
Finite element model setup: 250 eight-node isoparametric elements and 4x25 six-node joint elements.
dependent_variables: Normalized beam center displacement v_0 / v_0^infty (normalized by the displacement at infinite interface stiffness).
Normalized crack extension force g / g_infty in the compliance test.
Critical dimensionless horizontal buckling stress sigma^*.
Relative curvature tensor kappa_{ijk}^rel and relative deformation tensor gamma_{ij}.
Stress tensor sigma_{ij} and couple stress tensor m_{ijk}.
Cross-sectional macro- and micro-bending moments (M, m) and shear forces (Q, T).

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Incorporating layer bending stiffness proportional to the relative deformation gradient allows a laminated continuum model to eliminate spurious couple stresses during pure bending and correctly reduce to an isotropic standard continuum when interfacial slip vanishes.

For a simply supported layered beam subjected to point loading, the relative gradient beam theory predicts center displacements within less than 5% relative difference compared to finite element simulations across intermediate interfacial shear stiffnesses.
The influence of micromoments and couple stresses on layered beam bending becomes quantitatively significant when [E / (12 * k_s * h * (1 - nu^2))] * [1 + (h/t)^2] is much greater than 1.

In buckling analysis of layered systems, the relative gradient model smoothly bridges between the Euler buckling stress for a solid beam in plane strain at infinite interface stiffness and the buckling stress of individual uncoupled laminates as interface shear stiffness approaches zero.

Including individual layer bending stiffness preserves the mathematical uniqueness of boundary value solutions when interface material yields and tangential shear stiffness vanishes, preventing differential singularities that occur in standard continuum formulations.

The relative gradient formulation provides closed-form analytical expressions for the crack extension force in a compliance test configuration, generalizing classical solutions across variable interface stiffness values.

future_work: Application of the relative gradient ideas to regular dislocation structures with couple stresses and single slip in crystalline materials.
Extension to granular material theories with isotropic or multidirectional contact distributions where interfacial slip occurs across multiple orientations.
Comprehensive formulation of large-deformation problems without neglecting higher-order geometric nonlinearities.
independent_variables: Dimensionless interface shear modulus ratio ln(G / (k_s * h)) and parameter G / (k_s * h).
Geometric aspect ratios of the beam including thickness-to-length ratio t/L and layer-to-beam thickness ratio h/t.
Layer material elastic properties: Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio nu.
Interface constitutive properties: normal interface stiffness k_n, shear interface stiffness k_s, friction angle phi, and cohesion c.
Applied mechanical boundary loads: central point load P and axial prestress sigma_0.
Buckling mode number n.
Spatial coordinates x_1 (longitudinal axis) and x_2 (transverse/normal axis).
limitations_inferred: The theory was evaluated only on idealized 1D beam and 2D planar problems (simply supported beam bending, compliance test, buckling) without evaluation on complex 3D structures or under dynamic loading conditions.
No physical experimental mechanics tests were conducted on real specimens; validation relied entirely on comparisons with analytical limits and numerical finite element simulations.
The beam formulations assume unidirectional layer stacking and slip along a single axis, which may not capture multidirectional sliding, delamination, or complex contact evolution.

While the interface model includes elasto-plastic frictional sliding, the quantitative benchmark examples focused primarily on varying linear elastic interface shear stiffness rather than large cyclic post-yield frictional sliding regimes.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The moment-curvature constitutive relation based on relative deformation gradients is purely ad hoc and constitutive by nature.
The deformation measures gamma_{ij} and kappa_{ijk} are valid only for infinitesimal deformations.
The presented large deformation variant assumes that geometric nonlinearities associated with higher-order deformation gradient derivatives and higher-order stresses are negligible.
The analytical buckling expression at the zero interface stiffness limit is approximate rather than exact because the (h/t)^2 denominator term includes only the leading terms from homogenization.
The zero lamination thickness limit cannot be taken in a straightforward manner because divergence occurs unless microscopic moduli are adjusted (renormalized).

The thickness parameter h in the continuum model does not necessarily match the physical layer thickness, functioning instead as an effective scale-dependent renormalized parameter calibrated against macroscopic moduli.
main_results: Developed a relative gradient continuum formulation for layered media where couple stresses are generated by gradients of interfacial relative slip, correctly vanishing in pure bending without interface slip.
Demonstrated exact agreement with classical Timoshenko beam theory at infinite interface stiffness and smooth interpolation to the decoupled layer solution at zero interface stiffness.

Verified that the 1D generalized beam model predicts center deflection within 5% of finite element solutions (utilizing 250 eight-node elements and 100 joint elements) across intermediate interface stiffness regimes.
Proved that incorporating layer bending stiffness maintains solution uniqueness and eliminates differential singularities upon interface yielding and loss of tangential stiffness.
Derived analytical solutions for the compliance test crack extension force and beam buckling load as functions of dimensionless interfacial shear stiffness.
modeling_methods: Relative gradient continuum theory incorporating relative spin and relative curvature tensors.
Virtual work principle formulation for infinitesimal deformation and incremental virtual work for finite deformation.
Elasto-plastic interface constitutive modeling with friction angle and cohesion (Mohr-Coulomb type criterion and plastic potential).
Generalized 1D layered beam theory incorporating macro- and micro-element equilibrium and kinematic rotations.
Analytical derivation of crack extension force for laminated beam compliance testing.
Homogenization and scale-dependent parameter renormalization for layered media.
Finite element analysis using 250 eight-node isoparametric continuum elements and 4x25 six-node joint elements.
Eigenvalue buckling analysis for layered beam columns under axial prestress.
performance_metrics: Normalized center displacement v_0 / v_0^infty.
Relative percentage difference between gradient beam model predictions and finite element calculations (less than 5%).
Normalized crack extension force g / g_infty.
Critical dimensionless horizontal buckling load/stress sigma^*.
Asymptotic recovery of exact classical limits at zero and infinite interface shear stiffness.
possible_gap_implications: The relative gradient continuum framework provides a rigorous basis for modeling layered structures with tunable interfacial shear stiffness, but it was not applied to soft robotics, variable-stiffness layer jamming devices, or continuum manipulators.

The analytical modeling of interfacial slip resistance and individual layer bending moments could help bridge the gap in soft robotics between computationally heavy finite element models and oversimplified beam theories for layer-jammed variable-stiffness actuators.

The lack of physical experimental validation highlights a gap where experimental mechanics studies on multi-layer variable-stiffness prototypes could validate the predictive accuracy of the relative gradient model under real frictional and contact conditions.

The neglect of higher-order geometric nonlinearities and assumption of linear elastic layer materials present a gap for soft robotic applications that undergo hyperelastic response and large deformations.
paper.research_objective: To derive a consistent continuum theory for layered materials within a relative gradient framework that accounts for the bending stiffness of individual layers—ensuring couple stresses vanish during pure bending and reducing to an isotropic standard continuum upon vanishing interface slip—and to evaluate its accuracy against exact analytical limits and finite element simulations for layered beam bending, compliance, and buckling.
paper.research_problem: Standard continuum models of laminated materials struggle to represent short wavelength phenomena and interfacial slip, while earlier Cosserat-type models predict non-zero couple stresses during pure bending and fail to reduce to an isotropic continuum when interface slip vanishes. Furthermore, conventional models exhibit differential singularities and loss of uniqueness when interface yielding causes tangential stiffness to vanish.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Omitting interfacial strain energy terms in variational derivations (Hamilton's principle) of homogenized zig-zag plate models causes large errors (60% to 80% on interface shear tractions) and artificial slip-locking for intermediate interface stiffnesses.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A two-length-scales kinematic displacement field combined with a priori interfacial continuity constraints homogenizes multilayered plates with imperfect interfaces into five or six global kinematic variables independent of layer count.

For multilayered plates with compliant sliding interfaces, internal shear stresses derived directly from kinematic strain tend to zero as interface compliance increases, requiring generalized shear force and generalized shear strain concepts to account for cross-sectional transverse equilibrium.

In thin plates (L/h = 10) with sliding interfaces, the corrected first-order homogenized theory yields longitudinal displacement and transverse shear stress distributions that match exact 2D elasticity across all bonding states from fully bonded to fully debonded.

future_work: Validation of the proposed homogenized formulation for general mixed-mode interfaces involving normal opening separation and contact (BN != 0 and w_jump != 0) (page 18).

Formulation of an interfacial-stiffness-dependent shear correction factor to accurately predict transverse displacements in thick, highly orthotropic plates with very compliant interfaces (pages 15, 17, 18, 25).
Resolution of boundary region inconsistencies in clamped plates under intermediate interface stiffnesses (page 13).
Application of the affine interface formulation to progressive delamination modeling with nonlinear cohesive laws approximated as piecewise linear functions (pages 2, 4, 18).
Extension of the corrected formulations to buckling, vibration, blast, impact, and thermo-magneto-electro-mechanical loading problems (page 18).
independent_variables: Dimensionless interfacial stiffness K2*h / (EL * (L/h)^2) and dimensionless compliance B2*ET / h (pages 14, 16, 17).
Plate aspect ratio L/h (values examined: L/h = 4, 5, 10) (pages 14, 16, 17).
Laminate layup and number of layers (two-layer unidirectional 0/0 plate; three-layer symmetric cross-ply 0/90/0 plate) (page 14).
Through-thickness coordinate x3 / h (pages 14-17).
Longitudinal coordinate x2 along the plate length (pages 14-16).
Degree of layer orthotropy and dimensionless shear stiffness GLT / (EL * (L/h)^2) (pages 14, 16, 17).
limitations_inferred: The paper is purely theoretical and analytical/computational; no experimental validation or physical mechanical testing was conducted on physical specimens.
The affine formulation requires piecewise linear discretization for nonlinear cohesive fracture laws, which may require tracking multiple distinct loading/unloading branches.

The analytical benchmark and validations are restricted to 1D/2D cylindrical bending geometries and shallow shell/plate assumptions, leaving complex 3D boundary geometry effects and localized 3D stress concentrations unverified.
Although dynamic elastokinetic equations are derived via Hamilton's principle, all validation examples and benchmarks are restricted to static loading cases.

Hamilton's elastokinetic principle / principle of virtual work including interfacial strain energy terms from imperfect interfaces (pages 7, 19).

The transfer matrix method combined with an incremental superposition algorithm accurately predicts slip initiation, propagation length, and deflection of frictional laminated beams while avoiding the computational overhead and manual step interventions of nonlinear contact FEA.
Applied axial tension alters the structural response between cable-like and beam-like behavior; higher tension localizes shear near boundaries and loads, decreasing the slip propagation length.

constitutive_assumptions: The parallel wire cable cross section is idealized into layered rectangular composite cross sections preserving the total height and total wire cross-sectional area.

Cross sections with differing layer widths are transformed into an equivalent section with uniform unit width (width = 1) by scaling Young's modulus (E_i = b_i * E_i') to maintain identical longitudinal stiffness (EA) and bending stiffness (EI).

Interfacial slip is permitted at every layer interface, and the interactive shear force is assumed to be linearly proportional to the relative slip via a slip rigidity parameter (V_si = k_i * \Delta u_i).
Deflection and curvature of each layer are assumed identical with no lateral separation between adjacent layers (v^(i+1) = v^(i) and \sigma_y^(i+1) = \sigma_y^(i)).
Each layer is assumed to be in an in-plane stress state governed by isotropic linear elasticity under small-strain deformation with a finite initial axial tensile stress.
The classical Euler-Bernoulli plane section assumption holds only within each individual wire layer, but is invalid across the composite cross section as a whole due to inter-wire slips.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Bending stiffness of layered wire cables varies continuously between an upper bound (no-slip bonded state, EI_max) and a lower bound (full-slip state, EI_min) based on the interfacial anti-slip ability and contact effects among wires.

In the absence of axial tension, transverse bending of wire cables demonstrates bilinear behavior consisting of an initial stiff stick stage followed by a slip stage after exceeding a critical deflection threshold of approximately 1 mm (critical curvature around 6 \times 10^-6 m^-1).
Axial tension increases the interfacial slip rigidity through Poisson-effect radial tightening, which suppresses relative wire slip and linearizes the bending force-deflection response.

Treating multi-wire assemblies as a plane-stress laminated beam with compliant shear interfaces allows simultaneous closed-form prediction of global flexural deflection and local interlayer slip and stress discontinuities using the state space method.

Interfacial relative slip in bent wire bundles is zero at the mid-span line of symmetry and peaks at the simply supported ends, with the ratio of slips across interfaces transitioning from unity at low slip rigidity to the ratio of static moments at high slip rigidity.

The Euler-Bernoulli plane section assumption breaks down across the composite cross section of slipping wire bundles, leading to stepped displacement and stress profiles along the cross-sectional depth.

experimental_setup: Validation against three-point quasi-static bending experiments of structural cables from literature (Chen et al. [57])
Simply supported cable specimens with span length L = 820 mm
Three parallel wire cable cross-section configurations tested: 37\phi7, 55\phi7, and 61\phi7
Axial tensile preload Tx0 applied at both cable ends at four levels: 0 kN, 50 kN, 80 kN, and 100 kN
Quasi-static concentrated transverse load P progressively applied at mid-span to record force-deflection curves
future_work: Extending the analytical laminated beam formulation to incorporate realistic nonlinear inter-wire interaction and slip behaviors once the exact nonlinear mechanisms among wires are experimentally clarified.
Applying the proposed analytical model to more complex cable studies, including dynamic properties and fatigue life predictions.
independent_variables: Cable cross-section configuration (37\phi7, 55\phi7, 61\phi7)
Applied axial tensile force Tx0 (0 kN, 50 kN, 80 kN, 100 kN)
Quasi-static mid-span concentrated vertical load P
Interfacial slip rigidity k (calibrated linearly with average tensile stress as k = 7\bar{\sigma} + 50 MPa)
Longitudinal position coordinate along the span (x or \xi = x/L)
Vertical position coordinate across the cable depth (y or \zeta = y/H)
limitations_inferred: The model is formulated specifically for parallel wire cables and cannot be directly applied to helically wound wire ropes, strands, or twisted tendons where torsional-bending coupling is significant.

The validation was limited to quasi-static, simply supported three-point bending at a single span length (L = 820 mm), leaving dynamic flexural response and complex end clamping conditions unverified experimentally.
Wear, plasticity, fretting fatigue, and wire cross-section flattening under severe local contact pressure are not captured by the elastic laminated beam representation.
Transforming circular wires into continuous rectangular layers neglects discrete transverse line/point contact kinematics and out-of-plane spreading.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The actual interactions among wires are nonlinear and more intricate than the simplified linear shear-slip relationship assumed in the model, and the exact nonlinear interaction behavior remains unclear.
The slip rigidity parameter is semi-empirical and must be calibrated through experimental test data.
The model assumes identical deflection and curvature for all layers and neglects lateral separation between layers.
main_results: The state-space Fourier series expansion converges rapidly, with truncation error below 0.2% when 15 or more terms are retained.
Cable bending stiffness is bounded between an upper bound (no-slip state, EI_max) and a lower bound (full-slip state, EI_min) depending on interfacial slip rigidity.

Under zero axial tension, cables exhibit pronounced bilinear force-deflection behavior; a bilinear modeling strategy capturing a stick-to-slip transition at a critical curvature of approximately 6 \times 10^-6 m^-1 (around 1 mm mid-span deflection) matches experimental data significantly better than a purely linear model.

Under axial tension, the force-deflection response linearizes due to Poisson-induced clamping, and a linear slip rigidity strategy (k = 7\bar{\sigma} + 50 MPa) agrees closely with experimental curves.

In the absence of tension, the bending stiffness during the initial stick stage is below 50% of EI_max, and in the slip stage is roughly 50% greater than EI_min, indicating that wires are neither fully bonded nor completely frictionless.
Interfacial slips are antisymmetric along the cable length, vanishing at the mid-span and reaching maximum values at the ends.

The ratio of slips at higher interfaces relative to the first interface follows an exponential relation with slip rigidity, approaching 1 for low rigidity and the ratio of sectional static moments for high rigidity.

Cross-sectional displacements and bending stresses are stepped and asymmetric about the global neutral axis, confirming the invalidity of the classical plane section assumption across the entire cable section.

State space method for multilayered composite beams
Fourier series expansion of state variables
Layer-by-layer transfer matrix method
Linear slip rigidity modeling strategy (k = \lambda\bar{\sigma} + k0)
Bilinear modeling strategy for stick-to-slip state transition based on critical curvature/deflection threshold
performance_metrics: Fourier series truncation error (< 0.2% for 15 terms)
Force-deflection curve agreement with experimental measurements
Deflection magnification coefficient (DMC, \delta = f_slip / f_no-slip)
Equivalent bending stiffness coefficient (EBSC, \gamma = 1/\delta)
Critical curvature threshold (\kappa \approx 6 \times 10^-6 m^-1)
Interfacial slip ratio (\Delta u_i / \Delta u_1)
possible_gap_implications: The mechanism of tunable bending stiffness via variable interlayer slip and axial tension could inform the design of friction-based variable-stiffness continuum robots and tendon-driven catheters.

The state space transfer matrix formulation offers a computationally efficient analytical alternative to complex 3D finite element contact models for simulating multi-wire tendon packs or layered flexible backbones.

The identified bilinear stick-to-slip transition implies that tendon-driven soft manipulators operating at low tension may experience sudden stiffness drops and non-smooth actuation profiles upon exceeding critical curvature thresholds.

paper.research_problem: Bending of parallel wire cables involves intricate inter-wire slips and interactive forces that invalidate classical Euler-Bernoulli beam theory; existing analytical models often neglect friction and slip or cannot quantify slip directly, while finite element contact models and physical experiments are computationally or experimentally expensive and typically capture only global force-deflection responses rather than local deformations and stresses.

contact and friction effects between adjacent wire layers
clench effect of the protective cable sheath providing initial slip rigidity (k0)
Poisson-effect radial tightening under axial tensile stress increasing interfacial slip rigidity

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: An equivalent single layer / Zig-Zag model can be extended to dynamic wave propagation in multilayered plates with imperfect sliding interfaces by introducing displacement slip jumps governed by interface compliance matrices into Woodcock parameters.

Interfacial sliding defects cause a frequency shift of bending wavenumbers, equivalent flexural rigidity transitions, and maximum damping peaks toward lower frequencies by facilitating transverse shear between layers.
Extensional wave modes are entirely unaffected by interfacial sliding because interface shear stresses couple only to rotational and shear kinematic variables in the plate formulation.

Equivalent damping based on Love-Kirchhoff plate theory overestimates damping when shear deformation occurs, requiring correction using the ratio of group velocity to phase velocity to compute true energy damping.
An interfacial sliding defect can shift the equivalent flexural rigidity curve in a manner indistinguishable from an eight-fold reduction in core Young's modulus under a perfect interface assumption.

Asymptotic flexural rigidity limits at low frequency and high frequency (approaching the sum of skin rigidities) remain unaffected by moderate sliding defects, altering only when interfaces approach total debonding.
The sensitivity of the panel's dynamic frequency shift to interface compliance increases with a higher core-to-skin thickness ratio and decreases with a higher skin-to-core stiffness ratio.

future_work: Incorporating third-order vertical displacement fields to better describe transverse shear stress variations, particularly under severe debonding conditions.
Incorporating dilatational motion to extend the model's validity to higher frequencies and capture breathing modes.
Modeling interfacial openings to account for normal separation and out-of-plane defect modes.
Implementing frequency-dependent and spatially varying interface parameters.
Developing nonlinear interface constitutive relations, including piecewise linear models.
Validating the modeling methodology experimentally on physical sandwich panels with physical bonding defects.
Applying the equivalent dynamic framework to Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) for detecting adhesive defects and tracking structural aging.

Interface condition / interface compliance parameter (perfectly bonded B = 0 vs. imperfect sliding B = 5e-10 m/Pa)
Layer thicknesses (skin thickness, core thickness, and core-to-skin thickness ratio)

limitations_inferred: No physical experiments were conducted in the study to validate the predicted dynamic effects of sliding interfaces on physical sandwich structures.
The linear compliance interface formulation does not capture nonlinear friction phenomena such as stick-slip, amplitude dependence, or normal-pressure-dependent contact mechanics.
The formulation assumes infinite plate dimensions and planar wave propagation, omitting finite boundary conditions, clamping constraints, and edge reflections.
Interfacial sliding is modeled without frictional energy loss unless an imaginary compliance component is manually assigned, which may underestimate damping in dry sliding contacts.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Dilatational motion is not included in the model, defining the high-frequency limit of the framework and potentially affecting predictions even in the 200 to 500 Hz range.
Normal interfacial openings are neglected, preventing the representation of normal debonding or gap formation between layers.
Interface compliance and stiffness parameters are assumed to be constant across space and frequency.
Vertical displacement is assumed linear through the thickness, forcing transverse shear stresses to remain constant through each layer rather than higher-order.
The model derivation is presented under isotropic layer assumptions for simplicity (though extendable to anisotropy).
The Love-Kirchhoff equivalent damping formulation overestimates damping in shear-dominated regimes, requiring correction by group-to-phase velocity ratios.
The methodology has not been validated or applied experimentally on physical sandwich panels.
main_results: Interfacial sliding introduces in-plane displacement discontinuities (jumps) at the interfaces, making layer deformation increasingly independent and facilitating transverse shear.
The presence of sliding interfaces causes the frequency-dependent dynamic response curves (wavenumbers, flexural rigidity transition, and peak damping) to shift toward lower frequencies.
Extensional wavenumbers remain unaltered by sliding interfaces because interface shear stresses affect only shear and rotational variables.
Asymptotic flexural rigidity limits at low frequency and high frequency remain unchanged under moderate sliding defects, altering only when interfaces approach complete debonding.
Lossless interfacial sliding shifts the frequency of peak damping toward lower frequencies without altering the maximum damping value itself.
The impact of interface compliance is magnified by a larger core-to-skin thickness ratio and attenuated by a larger skin-to-core stiffness ratio.
The dynamic equivalent model matches Shorter's Spectral Finite Element Method (SFEM) dispersion results and Ross-Kerwin-Ungar (RKU) asymptotic bonded and debonded limits.

A significant sliding defect shifts dynamic properties identically to an apparent eight-fold softening of the core, highlighting the risk of misidentifying bonding defects as degraded core properties.

Discontinuous interface kinematic formulation introducing displacement slip jumps

Reissner-Mindlin plate kinematic assumptions (bending, shearing, and membrane displacements)
Lagrangian mechanics and Hamilton's principle of least action to derive equations of motion
Woodcock parameter reformulation incorporating imperfection correction terms
Harmonic wave propagation formulation solved for complex wavenumbers via an 8th-order polynomial determinant
Love-Kirchhoff equivalent thin-plate formulation for frequency-dependent complex flexural rigidity
Energy damping formulation corrected by group-to-phase velocity ratio
Asymptotic flexural rigidity limit analysis at low and high frequencies
Benchmarking against Shorter's Spectral Finite Element Method (SFEM) and Ross-Kerwin-Ungar (RKU) model

Demonstrating that interface slip mimics core softening prevents erroneous material parameter extraction during experimental vibro-acoustic characterization.
Providing an analytical equivalent plate formulation enables rapid parameter sweeps and optimization without computationally demanding 3D finite element meshes.
The absence of experimental validation and lack of nonlinear frictional contact modeling remains an unaddressed gap for practical engineering and soft robotic structural design.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Interlayer slipping invalidates the classical plane cross-section assumption, causing effective bending stiffness to decrease from the bonded limit Dplane_bend to the unbonded limit Dplane_bend / N^2 as interlayer shear interaction vanishes.

Under the Elastic Shear Stress (ESS) interface model, the governing axisymmetric equilibrium equations yield closed-form deflection and slip profiles in terms of modified Bessel functions, resulting in a strictly linear elastic load-displacement relation with slope fE(N, κE).

Under the Critical Shear Flow (CSF) interface model, deformation proceeds through three distinct stages—completely sticking (0 <= p <= pa), partially slipping with an advancing slip front r0 (pa < p <= p0), and completely slipping (p > p0)—producing a quasi-bilinear-hardening load-displacement curve.

Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations validate analytical predictions of slip displacement evolution, deflection curves, bending stiffness correction functions, and load-displacement responses across various layer counts and shear factors.

Because slip distribution depends strongly on bending configuration, applying 1-D bending models to 2-D axisymmetric bubbling test data underestimates interlayer shear moduli by approximately five-fold (0.0217 vs 0.1105 GPa for graphene, 0.0544 vs 0.2737 GPa for hBN, and 0.1135 vs 0.5708 GPa for MoS2).

Multilayered structures can be parametrically designed for tailored stiffness responses: ESS interfaces allow continuous adjustment of linear bending stiffness via shear factor κE, while CSF interfaces allow tuning of bilinear hardening post-yield slope (1/N^2) and threshold load via shear strength τ0.

Finite Element Method (FEM) numerical simulation setups were used to validate the theoretical models across discrete values of layer numbers and dimensionless shear factors.

Incorporating the strain energy contribution of imperfect interfaces into the Principle of Virtual Works allows homogenized zigzag models with affine traction laws to describe layered plates across the full range from fully bonded to fully debonded states using only a small set of displacement variables.

In multilayered plates with imperfect or cohesive interfaces, the gross internal stress resultant directly related to the derivative of the bending moment is a generalized transverse shear force (Q_2^g) rather than the standard transverse shear force of single-layer theory (Q_2^b).

The apparent inconsistency where shear force drops to zero at the clamped edge of a cantilever plate in prior zigzag models is explained by geometric boundary conditions forcing Q_2^b to zero, whereas the generalized shear force Q_2^g correctly equals the applied external force along the entire length.

In very thick, highly anisotropic plates with compliant interfaces, transverse shear deformations are underestimated due to the assumed continuity between interfacial tractions and shear stresses, indicating the need for an interface-stiffness-dependent shear correction factor.

Enforcing continuity conditions solely on homogenized displacement variables leads to localized layer displacement incompatibilities and inaccurate layer stresses in a small boundary zone (~L/50) near delamination crack tips, while gross stress resultants and couples remain accurate.

future_work: Derivation and implementation of a problem-dependent shear correction factor (K2) that depends on interfacial properties to improve transverse shear deformation and boundary region predictions (pages 2, 7, 10).
Application of the generalized formulation accounting for interfacial opening (Mode I / mixed-mode) to cohesive delamination problems under general mixed-mode loading conditions (page 2).
Extension and utilization of the homogenized plate formulation for broader fracture mechanics problem solving in multilayered structures (pages 2, 10).
independent_variables: In-plane spatial coordinate x2 along the plate span (pages 2, 4).
Through-thickness spatial coordinate x3 (pages 2, 4).
Interfacial tangential stiffness K_S (or compliance B_S), evaluated from fully debonded to fully bonded limits (pages 3, 7-9).
Plate aspect ratio / normalized thickness (e.g., L/h = 4 for thick plates, L/h = 10 for cantilever plates) (pages 2, 8).
Layer stacking sequence, individual layer thicknesses, and orthotropic material elastic constants (EL, ET, GLT, GTT, nu_LT, nu_TT) (pages 8-9).
Boundary condition types (simply supported versus clamped edges) (pages 2, 8-9).
Applied transverse mechanical loading (sinusoidal distributed surface load vs. tip concentrated force F) (pages 8-9).
Interface bonding status along the length (e.g., bonded for x2 in [0, L/2] and debonded for x2 in [L/2, L]) (page 9).
limitations_inferred: The formulation and examples presented are limited to cylindrical bending (one-dimensional beam/wide plate kinematics in plane strain) and do not address two-dimensional plate deformations involving biaxial bending or twisting.
The study does not examine robotic mechanisms, soft robotic components, variable stiffness actuators, or active continuum systems.
No physical experiments were conducted; model validation relies entirely on comparisons with exact 2D elasticity solutions and discrete-layer numerical models.
Dynamic inertial effects and interfacial separation/opening (Mode I) were omitted in the specific plate examples analyzed.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The assumption that interfaces are completely rigid against Mode I opening relative displacements is strictly valid only for pure Mode II conditions and cannot represent general mixed-mode cohesive delamination without applying the more general formulation (page 2).

For very thick, highly anisotropic plates with compliant interfaces, shear deformations are underestimated when calculating transverse displacements due to assumed continuity between interfacial tractions and shear stresses (page 2).

The transverse shear stress sigma_23 obtained directly from constitutive equations is constant across the thickness and fails to represent the true stress distribution except in homogeneous, perfectly bonded plates (page 7).

Boundary regions exist near clamped edges and delamination crack tips where layer-level displacements and stresses are inaccurate (displaying displacement incompatibility across the interface) because boundary and continuity conditions are imposed only on global/homogenized variables (pages 8-10).

Fracture mechanics predictions cannot rely on local crack-tip stress fields and must instead be calculated using gross stress resultants and couples evaluated at the boundary of the crack-tip region (page 10).
main_results: Formulated equilibrium equations for multilayered wide plates with imperfect/cohesive interfaces deforming in cylindrical bending, showing that the gross stress resultant directly related to the bending moment is a generalized transverse shear force Q_2^g rather than the conventional transverse shear force Q_2^b (pages 6, 8, 10).

Clarified apparent literature inconsistencies in zigzag models of clamped beams, proving that Q_2^g correctly equals the external applied force F along the entire span, whereas Q_2^b artificially vanishes at clamped edges due to geometric constraints (pages 2, 8, 10).

Accurately predicted in-plane displacements and through-thickness stress distributions across arbitrary interface stiffnesses (from fully bonded to fully debonded) using only three generalized displacement functions for wide plates (pages 1-2, 5, 8).

Identified localized boundary zones near clamped edges and delamination tips (crack-tip zone size approximately L/50 for unidirectionally reinforced laminates) where layer-level stresses and displacements lose accuracy due to homogenized continuity enforcement, while gross stress resultants remain accurate (pages 8-10).

Demonstrated that accurate energy release rates and stress intensity factors can be derived for delaminated plates using crack-tip gross stress resultants and couples despite localized crack-tip displacement incompatibilities (pages 9-10).
modeling_methods: Homogenized first-order zigzag plate theory using a two-length-scales displacement field combining global first-order shear deformation kinematics, layerwise zigzag functions, and interface displacement jumps (pages 3-5).
Affine (piecewise linear) interfacial traction laws relating interfacial shear stresses to sliding displacement jumps (pages 3-4).
Principle of Virtual Works formulated with the inclusion of interface traction strain energy to derive weak-form equilibrium equations and boundary conditions (pages 5-6).
Generalized transverse shear force formulation modifying the classical bending moment-shear force equilibrium relation (pages 6, 8).
A posteriori determination of transverse shear and transverse normal stresses via local 2D equilibrium equations using bending stresses (pages 7-9).
Application of a shear correction factor (K2) to account for thickness-wise transverse shear deformation (page 7).
Analytical evaluation of energy release rates and stress intensity factors based on gross crack-tip stress resultants and couples (pages 9-10).
performance_metrics: Accuracy of predicted displacement and stress fields compared to exact 2D elasticity solutions and discrete-layer model predictions (pages 2, 8-9).
Equilibrium consistency of the generalized transverse shear force Q_2^g with the external equilibrant force F across the plate span (pages 2, 8).
Size of the localized boundary zone near clamped supports and delamination crack tips where localized inaccuracies occur (pages 8-10).
Accuracy of energy release rate and stress intensity factor predictions at delamination crack tips (pages 9-10).
possible_gap_implications: The homogenized zigzag approach with generalized shear resultants could potentially provide computationally efficient reduced-order modeling for flexible multi-layer continuum structures with sliding interfaces or layer-jamming variable-stiffness sheets, avoiding discrete-layer degrees of freedom.

Extending the formulation to incorporate finite deformations and mixed-mode interface separation could enable accurate modeling of flexible robotic grippers or soft manipulators subject to delamination, interlaminar slippage, or layered friction.
paper.research_objective: To restate and apply a homogenized zigzag plate theory to wide multilayered plates deforming in cylindrical bending with clamped edges and delaminations, introducing a generalized transverse shear force to resolve literature inconsistencies regarding shear force equilibrium and clarifying the model's capabilities and limitations for composite fracture mechanics.
paper.research_problem: Classical single-layer theories fail to capture severe through-thickness stress and displacement variations (zigzag patterns and interfacial jumps) in multilayered composites with imperfect interfaces or delaminations, while discrete-layer models require large numbers of unknowns scaling with layer count. Furthermore, existing zigzag theories for imperfect interfaces suffer from inconsistencies regarding gross stress resultants across varying interfacial stiffnesses, shear-locking effects, and apparent anomalies in transverse shear force at clamped edges.
paper.title: Influence of boundary conditions on the response of multilayered plates with cohesive interfaces and delaminations using a homogenized approach
